mercado.q: How do I get my money back?
mercado.a: Little by little. Each vendor pays me three hundred dollars a month for a stall. Fourteen stalls, that is four thousand two hundred a month. We pay the lease, the lights, the cleaning, and what is left goes back to the people who helped us start. It will not be a lot in one month. But it comes every month, like bread.

mercado.q: What if the vendors can't pay their rent?
mercado.a: Then we talk, like neighbors. Most of these vendors are family, or from the same towns as their neighbors. If one has a bad month, the others help, and they do not want to shame their cousin. I have run a bakery for more than forty years on this kind of trust. I have been paid late. I have almost never been not paid.

mercado.q: Why would shoppers come inside instead of buying on the sidewalk?
mercado.a: Because inside there are no tickets, no rain and no snow. Our customers already come for these vendors. Some ride the bus forty minutes for the chiles and tortillas. Inside, they can buy from fourteen stalls in one trip, find a notary, see the job board. And four in ten families here have no car, so they need what they buy close to home.

mercado.q: Is a market just for one group of people?
mercado.a: Anybody can buy a mango. But yes, it serves the families who already live here first. Our language, our foods, our way of finding work. That is not a wall around us. It is a front door. When someone new moves in, the mercado is where they learn what this neighborhood is.

mercado.q: Did your family choose to live in Eastgate?
mercado.a: At first, not completely. When my parents came, landlords in other neighborhoods would not rent to people like us. So they came where they could, where there were others like us. Later, we stayed because we wanted to. The church, the bakeries, people who speak Spanish. Some of it was choice and some of it was not. Both are true.

mercado.q: What happens to the old building?
mercado.a: Nothing bad. We clean it and we use it. The cornerstone stays, the signs stay. The stalls go inside the hall, where the women's circle used to meet. A building should be used by the people who live around it. An empty building just collects tickets and pigeons.

brewery.q: How do I get my money back?
brewery.a: Beer, mostly. Pints in the taproom, cans in local stores, food at the counter. If the taproom fills up the way I think it will, investors get paid back from profits over the first few years. My brother-in-law's spreadsheet says three. He's an accountant. Of taxes. But still, an accountant.

brewery.q: Isn't eight dollars a lot for a beer around here?
brewery.a: Yeah. It is. That's the part that keeps me up at night. A lot of my neighbors make around forty thousand a year. So we're doing a neighbors' night with lower prices, and the food comes from the bakery and the tortillería, so their money stays on the block. I'm not going to pretend new places don't change a street. They do.

Honestly? A mix. Young professionals, sure, the ones moving in. But also the folks I grew up with, my mom's salon customers, people who want somewhere to sit that isn't their kitchen. If I only get the newcomers, I've failed. If I only get my mom's friends, I've also failed, but more politely.

brewery.q: What will you do with the old signs and the cornerstone?
brewery.a: Keep them. Restore them. The cornerstone stays right where it is. We hire a real sign painter for the side wall, so you can see both layers: the Czech beer ad and the Spanish tortillería sign on top. That wall is the whole history of this block. Covering it would be like tearing pages out of a book.

brewery.q: Why name beers after local places?
brewery.a: Because a beer called Generic Pale Ale could come from anywhere. Ghost Sign Amber can only come from here. People want to feel connected to a place. But it has to be real. That's why I won't name anything after the Barrio. That's not a landmark, that's my neighbors' home. I'd be selling something that isn't mine.

brewery.q: What if neighbors don't want you there?
brewery.a: Some of them won't, at first. A couple already told me so, to my face. I'd rather hear it than not. So we hold a meeting every month, we hire from within ten blocks, and one wall is always for local artists. I grew up here. I'm not trying to replace anybody. I'm trying to be the porch everybody can sit on.

landing.q: How do I get my money back?
landing.a: Memberships and childcare. Forty-five dollars a month for the gym and co-working floor, six dollars an hour for childcare. The daycare alone will have a waitlist, because the nearest one is fourteen blocks away. I timed it. Investors get paid from monthly memberships, which come in every month whether it's raining or not.

landing.q: Why women only? Isn't that a small market?
landing.a: Half the population is not a small market. The gym and the co-working floor are women only because a lot of women here told us they don't feel comfortable in mixed gyms, or walking home late. The childcare and the language classes are open to everyone. I'm not closing a door. I'm opening one that's been missing.

landing.q: Do women really avoid this block?
landing.a: Seven in ten, according to the library's survey. The streetlight by the church is broken, the hall is boarded up, the sidewalk is empty after dark. So women cross the street or go around. That's what a space says about who belongs in it. We fix the light, we staff the side entrance, and that stretch of sidewalk changes.

landing.q: Has this building been used by women before?
landing.a: For ninety-eight years. My grandmother Anežka sewed there with the Wenceslas Women's Circle in the Czech years. My grandmother Lupe sat in the same chairs when it became the Círculo de Mujeres. Back then, a sewing circle was one of the few public places women could gather. The roles changed. The room didn't.

Mothers who need childcare so they can work. Women who work from home and need a desk that isn't the kitchen table. Teenagers in the English and Spanish classes. Grandmothers who used to come to the Círculo. I have a list of two hundred names already. I have a spreadsheet. I made the spreadsheet myself.

landing.q: What happens to the old building?
landing.a: It stays. We fix the windows, keep the brick and the cornerstone, and add a lit, staffed side entrance on Eighteenth. The room where the Circle met becomes the classroom. People should be able to look at that building and see who used it. Not erase that, add to it.

residences.q: How do I get my money back?
residences.a: Rents. Sixty units, twenty-four to thirty-one hundred a month, and ninety percent are already reserved. Lease up, refinance, cash out. Easy. Assuming construction stays on schedule, and the permits go through, and nobody makes a fuss. Which, honestly, why would they? It's a beautiful building.

Young professionals. Remote workers. People who appreciate a curated lifestyle. Not necessarily the, uh, existing demographic. But a rising tide lifts all boats! When new people move in, everything gets nicer. Coffee, retail, property values. The existing residents will love it, assuming they can stay.

Because it's a big empty box. Old brick, old wiring, old everything. Restoring it would cost a fortune and you can't fit sixty units in a church. But I hear you on history. That's why we're saving three bricks for the lobby wall. With a plaque. People love a plaque.

I'm sure they're excited. We put out a flyer. It has a QR code. Very modern. Did anyone scan it? Let me check my notes. We're skipping the community meeting because those things get emotional and slow down the timeline. Some voices might have concerns, but you can't please everyone.

residences.q: What if people in Eastgate fight the project?
residences.a: Then we have lawyers. Look, every project gets a little pushback. A historical society here, a residents' group there. Worst case, a delay. A few months. Maybe a year. The demand is real. Rents are up forty percent. People want in. A lawsuit is just a speed bump on the road to traction.

residences.q: Have you spent much time in Eastgate?
residences.a: Define "spent time." I've studied it closely on a real estate app for months. I did a drive-by on a Sunday. Great energy. Lots of murals. A little bakery that smelled incredible. I didn't go in. But I could feel the vibe. That's what I do. I feel the vibe, and then I activate it.

littleprague.q: How do I get my money back?
littleprague.a: Tour buses! Forty people a bus, every weekend, buying beer, pretzels, steins, and a feathered hat or two. The buses don't exist yet, technically. But once people hear there's a Little Prague, they'll come. Everybody loves a theme. I've been planning this since I was a kid. Well, since last spring.

Is it? It's close! It's from over there somewhere. Germany, Austria, Czech, it's all one big happy Central Europe, right? Cuckoo clocks, steins, yodeling. Okay, maybe yodeling is Swiss. The point is, it feels old world. Customers don't fact-check a pretzel.

Well, historically, Czech families! That's why the church has that beautiful Czech cornerstone. Now? I think it's, uh, more Spanish-speaking these days. Which is great! Very colorful. But the heritage is Czech, and I'm bringing the heritage back. The heritage society agrees. Nine out of eleven of them.

littleprague.q: Did you ask people who live here?
littleprague.a: I asked the heritage society, and they're very connected to the neighborhood. Emotionally. They live in the suburbs now, but their grandparents lived right here. That counts, doesn't it? I figure the current residents will come around once they hear the accordion. Nobody can stay mad at an accordion.

littleprague.q: What happens to the old signs on the wall?
littleprague.a: The Spanish one? We paint a big Czech flag over it. Fresh start! It's faded anyway, and it's not really part of the Czech story. Underneath there's an old Czech beer ad, so honestly, I'm putting the wall back the way it was. Kind of. With a flag.

littleprague.q: What will you call the neighborhood?
littleprague.a: Little Prague! It's right there in the heritage society newsletter. I'm petitioning to rename Eighteenth Street "Little Prague Way." I hear some locals call it the Barrio, and the realtors call it an Arts District, but Little Prague has a ring to it. Say it with me. Little Prague! See? Magical.
